name: Male Witchcraft and Gender Inversion (Challenges to the Feminization Thesis)
time_period: Early Modern (c.1450–1750); historiographical debate intensified from 1990s
primary_locale: Regionally variable: male-majority prosecution in Iceland, Estonia, Russia, Normandy, Finland; male-significant prosecution in eastern France, Burgundy, the Holy Roman Empire; female-majority prosecution in most English, Scottish, German, Swiss, Polish jurisdictions
scholarly_definition: Male witchcraft and gender inversion is the analytical concept addressing two interrelated questions: why were men prosecuted for witchcraft (in significant numbers, up to 25–50% of accused in several jurisdictions), and what the existence of substantial male prosecution reveals about gendered assumptions in demonological theory and prosecution practice. The concept challenges the 'feminization thesis' — the position associated with Anne Llewellyn Barstow (Witch Craze, 1994) and Carol Karlsen (The Devil in the Shape of a Woman, 1987) that witch prosecution was primarily a gendered campaign of persecution against women, driven by misogynist theology and social anxiety about female independence. While the demographic reality that approximately 75–80% of European accused were female is not disputed, the existence of substantial male prosecution in multiple jurisdictions — and male-majority prosecution in Iceland, Estonia, and parts of Russia — complicates any account that treats the gender dimension as simply or uniformly anti-female. The concept requires analysis of how demonological theory handled male witchcraft, what social types were targeted among male accused, and how gender interacted with other social variables (age, occupation, community conflict, regional tradition) in generating accusations.

intellectual_genealogy.feminization_thesis_origins: The feminist interpretation of witch prosecution, developed by Barbara Ehrenreich and Deirdre English (Witches, Midwives, and Nurses, 1973), Anne Llewellyn Barstow (Witch Craze, 1994), and Carol Karlsen (The Devil in the Shape of a Woman, 1987), argued that witch prosecution was fundamentally a campaign against women — specifically against female healers, independent widows, and those who challenged patriarchal authority. This thesis achieved wide popular and feminist scholarly influence.
intellectual_genealogy.male_prosecution_data: Regional studies from the 1980s onward accumulated data showing that male prosecution was not negligible: Midelfort (Witch Hunting in Southwestern Germany, 1972) noted male accused in German mass panics; Monter documented male-majority prosecution in Normandy; studies of Icelandic, Estonian, and Russian prosecution showed clear male predominance. By the 1990s the data challenged simple generalizations.
intellectual_genealogy.rowlands_schulte_synthesis: Alison Rowlands (Witchcraft Narratives in Germany: Rothenburg, 1561–1652, 2003; Witchcraft and Masculinities in Early Modern Europe, 2009) and Rolf Schulte (Man as Witch: Male Witches in Central Europe, German 2000, English 2009) provided the most sustained scholarly analysis of male witchcraft, examining how demonological theory accommodated male practitioners and what social dynamics generated male accusations.

clark_intellectual_analysis: Clark's intellectual history is relevant to male witchcraft in a specific way: he analyzes the demonological construction of female susceptibility (the elaboration of why women were more vulnerable to demonic seduction than men) as a coherent theological argument rather than simple misogyny. For Clark, the feminization of witchcraft in demonological theory reflected the gendered application of specific theological categories — female inconstancy, carnal desire, susceptibility to deception — that were internally coherent within the demonological system. Male witchcraft thus posed a conceptual problem for demonology that some theorists resolved by assigning males a different role (active sorcerers or leaders rather than seduced victims) and that others managed by downplaying the gendered dimension of their frameworks. The theoretical accommodation of male witchcraft is as revealing of demonological logic as the feminization thesis itself.
hutton_social_analysis: Hutton (The Witch, 2017) insists on taking the demographic variation in male prosecution seriously as evidence against monolithic explanations. His analysis of cunning folk — the service-magic practitioners who constituted a significant proportion of accused across many jurisdictions — shows that cunning folk included substantial numbers of men; the professional healer or magical specialist was not uniformly female. Hutton also uses the cross-regional variation in male prosecution (male-majority in Iceland, male-significant in several Continental jurisdictions) to argue that witch prosecution was not a unitary phenomenon with a single gendered dynamic but a set of regionally specific practices shaped by different combinations of social, institutional, and cultural factors.
ginzburg_interrogation_analysis: Ginzburg's microhistorical approach foregrounds specific male practitioners — the benandanti of Friuli, the benandante leaders who were emphatically male — as evidence that the relationship between gender and witch prosecution was mediated through specific folk traditions and regional practices rather than through uniform demonological gendering. The Friuli benandanti (predominantly male in the early records, shifting to female over time as inquisitorial reinterpretation aligned them with the feminized witch) demonstrate how gender composition of prosecution could shift through interrogation dynamics rather than reflecting stable social categories.

actor_perspective.demonological_accommodation: Demonologists had to explain male witchcraft within frameworks that emphasized female susceptibility. Common solutions included: treating male witches as active sorcerers who seduced women rather than as passive victims of demonic seduction; emphasizing that heresy (which witchcraft implicated) was not gender-specific; or noting that Satan was an opportunist who targeted whoever was available, not only women.
actor_perspective.male_accused_social_profiles: Male accused in the data show different social profiles from female accused: herding communities in Iceland, Estonia, and Finland where male occupational specialization in outdoor work correlated with folk magic practice; court magicians and learned astrologers prosecuted for learned magic; men accused through denunciation cascade from female accused who named them as sabbath companions.
actor_perspective.community_perception: Communities that accused men of witchcraft often followed different accusation logic than communities accusing women: male accused were more likely to be identified through maleficium associated with their occupational role (herding magic, weather magic, competitive craft magic) than through the female-typical accusation types (illness of children, milk-stopping, domestic maleficium).

regional_variation_patterns.male_majority_jurisdictions: Iceland (80%+ male accused), Estonia (60%+ male), Russia (predominantly male through 17th century), Normandy (male-majority in specific periods): in these jurisdictions, folk magical practice was associated with male occupational roles (shamanistic healing, herding, fishing) rather than female domestic practice.
regional_variation_patterns.male_significant_jurisdictions: Several German territories, Burgundy, eastern France show male prosecution rates of 30–50%, substantially higher than the European average; typically associated with learned magic prosecution or with denunciation cascade from female-initiated panics in which male leaders were implicated.
regional_variation_patterns.female_dominant_jurisdictions: England, Scotland, the Swiss Confederation, most German territories: female accused constitute 75–90% of the total; these jurisdictions show the social profile most consistent with the charity-refusal model and domestic maleficium accusation pattern.

gender_inversion_in_demonology.theoretical_problem: The feminization of witchcraft in demonological theory created a conceptual problem when men were prosecuted. If women were peculiarly susceptible to demonic seduction because of their carnal weakness and inconstancy, what explained male witches?
gender_inversion_in_demonology.demonological_solutions: Solutions included: (1) treating male witches as active partners rather than passive seduced victims, reversing the gender dynamic; (2) emphasizing that heresy was gender-neutral even if susceptibility was not; (3) arguing that exceptional men — particularly the learned, the proud, or the occupationally exposed — were vulnerable in ways analogous to women's general vulnerability.
gender_inversion_in_demonology.inversion_logic: Some demonologists used gender inversion as part of a broader inversionary logic: the sabbath involved the inversion of all natural hierarchies, including gender hierarchies, such that men might take female roles and women male roles. This allowed male prosecution to be accommodated within a framework that otherwise emphasized female susceptibility.

historiographical_significance: The male witchcraft evidence is historiographically important because it disciplines the feminist interpretation of witch prosecution without dismissing gender as an analytical category. Gender was unquestionably central to the social dynamics of accusation, the demonological construction of the witch, and the demographic patterns of prosecution — but 'gender' does not mean 'anti-female campaign.' The existence of multiple jurisdictions with substantial or predominant male prosecution means that any adequate account of witch prosecution must explain both the European-average female predominance and the regional male-majority exceptions; the account must identify which social conditions produced which gendered patterns rather than treating female prosecution as the explanatory norm and male prosecution as an anomaly. Rowlands' and Schulte's work has established this as a productive research agenda.
scholarly_disagreement: Anne Barstow (Witch Craze, 1994) and Carol Karlsen (The Devil in the Shape of a Woman, 1987) argued for the primacy of misogynist motivation in prosecution; Barstow explicitly resisted attention to male prosecution as a distraction from the fundamental gendering of the phenomenon. Alison Rowlands (Witchcraft and Masculinities, 2009) and Rolf Schulte (Man as Witch, 2009) argued that male prosecution was substantial enough to require systematic analysis and that the feminization thesis was empirically inadequate. Hutton (The Witch, 2017) accepts Rowlands' and Schulte's evidence as compelling. Edward Bever (The Realities of Witchcraft and Popular Magic, 2008) argued that magic practice itself was not uniformly gendered and that the gendering of prosecution reflected social vulnerability factors that intersected with but were not reducible to sex. The debate remains active, particularly around the question of how to weight the European-average female predominance against regional male exceptions.
source_method: Alison Rowlands, Witchcraft and Masculinities in Early Modern Europe (ed., Palgrave Macmillan, 2009); Rolf Schulte, Man as Witch: Male Witches in Central Europe (Palgrave Macmillan, 2009); Anne Barstow, Witch Craze (HarperCollins, 1994); Carol Karlsen, The Devil in the Shape of a Woman (Norton, 1987); Ronald Hutton, The Witch (Yale University Press, 2017); Julian Goodare, The European Witch-Hunt (Routledge, 2016)
